hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text: The article “The Surprising Science of an All-Meat Diet,” which I published last week, is now on the most-read list for health articles and uptrending. This morning, I also finished an interview with a major newspaper in the United Kingdom that was interested in covering my perspective on saturated fat and cholesterol for National Cholesterol Month in the UK. A brief summary of my two major positions, because I don’t think they’re at all radical. I’ll be as concise as possible and link to more information below. 1) First, the carnivore diet is a tool, not a religion. It’s a mistake to present it as the best diet for humans or to make strong claims that go beyond the literature, such as that it will improve longevity. What we can say, accurately and humbly, is that it’s helping many people who have struggled with debilitating disorders and failed to find support through conventional approaches. We can also say that there is strong biological plausibility for many of the conditions for which it’s being used, including mental health disorders and autoimmune and inflammatory conditions. That’s not definitive proof. But it’s a possibility that deserves curiosity and compassion, not disdain. If you want the full scientific breakdown in video form: “The Strange Science of Eating Only Meat” youtu.be/WJnPDQ0XRXA 2) The second major point I’ll make is that CONTEXT matters. Meat is vilified largely because of its saturated fat and cholesterol content. However, when it comes to improving the cardiometabolic health of the general population, focusing on reducing saturated fat intake is like worrying about a mosquito when you’re being chased by a tiger. We now have randomized controlled trial data showing that low-carbohydrate ketogenic diets (despite typically being much higher in saturated fat and cholesterol) can provide greater improvements in many cardiometabolic risk markers than low-fat plant-based or Mediterranean-style diets higher in carbohydrates, particularly in people with obesity and insulin resistance. More here: staycuriousmetabolism.substack.com/p/a-major-tria … At the end of the day, I don’t fancy myself a carnivore fanboy. Just carnivore-curious and open-minded. That’s enough. P.S. There’s a tendency to make meat and diet unnecessarily political. Resist that tendency. What’s on my plate does not inform what I do at the ballot box. Stereotypes impair our ability to have thoughtful academic discourse. Ht/ @MikhailaFuller for her contribution (including the click-boost from her adorable baby) @EpochTimes

hits.text: I would not currently inject gray-market “research peptides.” The sourcing and quality-control risks are simply too high. The question isn’t whether peptides can work as signaling molecules (they can). It’s whether the vial contains the peptide it claims, at the stated dose, without microbial contamination, endotoxins, heavy metals, or peptide-related impurities. The FDA does not verify the safety, effectiveness, or quality of compounded drugs before marketing. Does that mean every compounded product is unsafe? No. But the safeguards are different. Until a specific research peptide has credible human evidence and a reliable source with transparent, independent testing, I would hold off.
hits.draft_en:

On a jobsite we don’t trust unmarked chemicals in a bottle. Same rule for your bloodstream.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: Alcohol is a hot topic (and an odd one for a guy like me to bring up--I've never had a drop in my life). But there is a relevant metabolic angle to it. If you drink most nights while trying to lose fat, you are regularly shutting down fat oxidation. The body clears alcohol first--it's a fuel that demands "priority boarding". While that is happening, fat burning drops hard, and more of the fat from your meals gets stored instead of burned. In one study, subjects drank about 96 g of alcohol in a day (roughly seven drinks), and 24-hour fat burning fell by about a third. That drop showed up whether the alcohol was added on top of their meals or swapped in for other calories. If you're looking to lose fat, I'd put alcohol at the top of the list of things to scrutinize. https://t.co/ZPitLMHSUj

hits.text: Bone health deserves attention before menopause, not just after. Roughly two-thirds of bone lost across the menopausal transition tends to occur within a three-year window - from one year before to two years after the final menstrual period. In a study of 862 women, bone density at the spine fell 10.6% over 10 years, but 7.4% was lost during this brief “transmenopause” period. Bone density of the femur fell 9.1%, with 5.8% lost during the same window. This is a reason for women to prioritize resistance and high-impact training around the menopause transition to prevent or slow the loss of bone density.
hits.draft_en:

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: I've been hearing people say glucose spikes don't matter as long as your average blood sugar looks fine. Your brain may disagree. Researchers put continuous glucose monitors on older adults for three days and then scanned their brains. The people whose glucose swung up and down the most over 30 minutes to 2 hours had less gray matter in the hippocampus (the brain's memory center) and did worse on cognitive tests. That held even after accounting for HbA1c (the three-month blood sugar average most doctors check). A normal average can hide plenty of spikes and crashes. I'd pay attention to what happens after meals, not just the number on your lab report. Ideally, keep the swings small. And really only a CGM can tell you this.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: Retatrutide has an advantage over other GLP-1-based drugs, and I think it comes down to glucagon, one of the more overlooked hormones in metabolism. Retatrutide adds glucagon on top of the GLP-1 and GIP signals. In the newly-released phase 3 TRIUMPH-1 trial, just published in NEJM (NCT05929066), adults with obesity took it for 80 weeks. At the top dose, people lost 25% of their body weight on average. More than a third lost at least 30%. Fasting insulin fell by more than half, something I always focus on, and over 90% of people with prediabetes ended up with normal blood sugar. Insulin tells the body to store fuel, and glucagon tells the body to burn it. In a separate study, researchers raised glucagon to normal physiological levels and found that the liver's mitochondria burned fuel 50 to 75% faster (PMID 39197461). In another study, a glucagon infusion raised energy expenditure by about 15% (PMID 26434748). Ideally, if you take it, protect your fat-free mass with resistance exercise and abundant protein and natural fats. I also feel strongly that any of these drugs needs to be viewed as a temporary crutch--use it to develop new habits (i.e., control carbs) and then taper off.
hits.draft_en:
New triple-agonist trial numbers are big. Bikman’s practical line matters more: if you use a tool like this, protect muscle.

Resistance work. Plenty of protein and real fats. Treat the jab as a temporary crutch while you build habits — not a forever lifestyle.

A labourer’s engine is muscle. Don’t shrink it to chase a scale number.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: If you're a young woman with insulin resistance, your brain may already be burning fuel like a 70-year-old's. Lean women in their 20s with PCOS/PMOS (polycystic ovary syndrome; a hormonal condition driven largely by insulin resistance, and one of the most common hormone disorders in women) had brains taking up 9 to 14% less glucose than women of the same age and weight. In healthy 70-year-olds, the same lab found drops of about 8 to 17%. The more insulin resistant a woman was, the less fuel her brain took in, and the pattern looked like early Alzheimer's disease. And it showed! Five of the seven scored low on memory tests. None were impaired yet, but these were women in their 20s. That matters because women already carry more of the Alzheimer's burden, making up nearly two-thirds of Americans living with it. Insulin resistance is one reason, and it can start decades earlier than anyone looks. None of these women were overweight, and their fasting blood sugar was close to normal. Their insulin told the real story. Ladies, if your doctor only checks glucose, ask for fasting insulin.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text: “Let Me Tell You About My Grift” A physician recently published a post using AI to analyze 12 health influencers and their supposed “grifts.” The individual is not worth platforming, but this it provides a useful springboard for a bigger conversation. The medical and informational ecosystems are evolving, creating a new niche for professional scientific communicators. If you watch the video below (10 minutes), you’ll see I’ve been transparent about why I’ve made the decisions I’ve made. My path was shaped by my own health story and a belief that I can do more good by educating people and empowering them on their health journeys than by writing prescriptions. But as this ecosystem evolves, some conventional clinicians seem uncomfortable that their professional influence is undermined by media educators. I’ve even had one old scholar cardiologist call me on the phone to complain “my patients are asking hard questions.” “Sorry?” I guess 🙈 But find it ironic when a clinician uses AI to label me a "grifter," with the precise claim being that I have a YouTube with 1.3 million subscribers and a paid newsletter. But I’ll do them one better. Let me tell you about my grift. Yes, I have a paid newsletter. #StayCurious Metabolism has become a top premium science newsletters on Substack. In 2026, we’ve held the #1 Rising Science position more often than every other science newsletter on the platform combined. Subscriptions start at the “hefty” price of $8 per month (less than 67 cents per letter). Why do people pay? Judging by comments from my community, it’s because the information gives them knowledge and tools to take greater control of their health; to understand their biology and approach conversations with physicians as informed partners rather than passive objects to be “compliant.” But here’s something else you might like to know. I’ve repeatedly turned down substantial financial offers (including six-figure deals) from companies whose products I didn’t believe in or organizations I wasn’t comfortable affiliating with, including pharmaceutical companies. I could have taken enough money from pharma to put a down payment on a house. I didn’t. Not a cent. My friends and colleagues can attest to that, and to the fact that I’ve been brutally transparent about my own health journey, even when doing so put my reputation at risk. I’m doing what I’m doing not because it’s the easy path, but because I believe it’s the path where I can make the biggest impact. I don’t say that to put myself above anyone else. As you’ll see in the video below, my entire social ecosystem is in medicine. And to me, these people are heroes. We need good clinicians. But there is a particular species of small, bitter clinician who comes online primarily to take shots at other people. My advice to them is simple: focus on being a great clinician. And if you’re going to get on the internet, focus on contributing something intellectually valuable. Because taking potshots at people who chose a different path isn’t intellectual contribution. It’s just a transparent signal that you want to be a thought “influencer” … but you’re not very good. And at the end of the day, the insecure medical bullies remind me exactly why I do what I do. outsiders.name: kiosa
outsiders.text: i genuinely don't understand why everyone isn't doing this yet Grok Bot watches your X timeline, figures out why other posts blow up and writes my next one before i even know what to post. i used to burn ~3 hours a day on this: scroll -> save posts -> check views -> dump ideas into notes -> stare at a blank draft -> repeat so i built a tiny X newsroom instead: -> Scout tracks ~18 accounts, skips replies, drops anything under 5K views, stars 10K+ -> then scans ~20 fresh AI posts from the last 48h to catch what the whole feed suddenly talks about -> it breaks down what worked: hook, keywords, structure, topic, tool, CTA -> Draft turns those patterns into a new post + a short video idea -> Board tracks everything: found, drafted, posted, still to do -> i fix whatever sounds dumb and hit Post myself. nothing auto-posts it doesn't invent trends. it reads what people already proved with their attention. one Claude bug-hunting post from this workflow did ~2.1M views. the math: ~3 hours/day back ~$1K/month not spent on assistants 1–2 posts/day without living in the feed a little AI employee with one job: find what works -> figure out why -> hand me something worth posting it's public and free

outsiders.name: JJ Englert
outsiders.text: I've taught 50 Claude trainings in the last 6 months, to engineers, execs, and operators at some of the best companies in the world. The part almost all of them still get wrong is how they set up their files. If Claude doesn't know you, your clients, or what you decided last week, every chat starts from zero. You end up explaining yourself over and over. My rough math: No file system, you're getting 20 to 30% of what Claude can do. A messy one, maybe 40 to 50%. A clean one your agents can move through fast, 80 to 90%. It doesn't matter if you code or not. If you write emails, build decks, manage clients, or run projects, it's the same problem and the same fix. It takes about 30 minutes, and it works in Claude Cowork, Claude Code, ChatGPT Work, and Codex. Your files are just folders on your computer, so any of them can read the same setup. It comes down to layers: Global instructions: for who you are and how you work. A top-level CLAUDE.md: that tells every new agent where things live. A CLAUDE.md in each client or project folder: so the agent gets up to speed without reading every file. A workspace map: so it goes straight to the right doc. Projects: so your chats build on each other. Set it up once and each new chat picks up where the last one left off. Learn it once and it works in every AI tool you use. I walked through my whole setup in this video, plus two free skills to build or audit yours (in comments below) Timestamps 00:00 You're only as good as your file system 02:00 What does Claude know about you? 04:11 The top-level CLAUDE.md 08:43 A CLAUDE.md in every subfolder 11:45 Free skills: create and audit your workspace 14:23 Global instructions 16:54 Projects stack your context 20:02 Before and after: an email 21:53 Before and after: slide decks 25:03 The 7 rules Enjoy 🍿
